1:
Two commentators independently stop on the opening verb, and both reach for Bengel: Ellicott quotes him to the effect that treason against Christians is denoted by this high-sounding word, and Robertson that the word is an argument in itself. The dispute begins with the epithet. Clarke hears a play on words, since Greek judges were called the righteous ones and are here named the unrighteous, and he thinks the sarcasm earned, given the corruption of manners at Corinth and the unlikelihood that a case touching Christians would be fairly decided. Barnes and Ellicott both refuse the moral reading: the word stands opposed to saints and means simply unbelievers, Barnes adding that Paul does not say equity could never be had from a heathen bench, Ellicott that neither word here conveys any essentially moral idea. Ellicott also explains why the fault was Gentile rather than Jewish, since Rome had granted the Jews liberty to settle their own disputes, as Gallio's remarks show, while Gentile converts naturally kept to the tribunals they had always used. Calvin meets the obvious objection by limiting the rebuke: a man summoned to a court may appear and defend himself, and only those are condemned who drag a brother there of their own accord.

What it means that the saints shall judge the world divides the chapter's largest body of comment. Barnes lays out four received answers and rejects the last: that they will be assessors to Christ, that they will judge by their example or as Christian magistrates, that they will judge errors in religion, or, with the Greek fathers, that their lives will furnish the matter of the world's deeper condemnation. Against that last he objects both that it is an unusual sense of the verb and that it does not meet the argument, since a holy example being the occasion of a heavier sentence gives no reason why a man should be fit to settle a dispute over property. Clarke, following Lightfoot, takes the world for the Jewish people and the promise for the eventual passing of civil government into Christian hands, and calls the assessor view clogged with absurdities, since the saints are themselves judged first and no thrones are needed for an approval the damned will not dispute. Ellicott reads it as the conquest of the world by Christianity, accomplished since by slower and more spiritual processes than were then expected. Calvin holds the assessor sense on the strength of the future tense.

On the angels Lightfoot's own note is the source the others draw from: the text says not that the saints shall judge them but that we shall, meaning the ministers of the gospel, who by preaching would spoil the devils of their oracles and idols and strip them of their dominion — and Clarke reproduces him almost word for word. Gill reaches the same conclusion by the Syriac, which reads that we are about to judge angels, a judgment already begun rather than reserved to the last day. Ellicott resists the whole approach, arguing that the contrast drawn in the next clause is not angels against men but angels against things, so the phrase is a climax about redeemed humanity rather than a hard fact about particular spirits. Calvin canvasses three readings before settling on apostate angels. The fourth verse turns on one unpointed verb, and Robertson states the fork plainly: read it as a question and the men of no account are the heathen, read it as a command and they are the least esteemed members of the church. Barnes takes the question, since Paul would hardly direct them to choose their least capable men. Lightfoot supplies the alternative from the five Jewish benches, the lowest being the unauthorised one chosen by the parties themselves.
5:
The question whether one wise man could be found is read as sarcasm turning to pathos. Robertson notes the double negative expects the answer yes, so that surely one such man exists, and that the phrase for deciding between brothers is doubly emphatic and even condensed, the second brother left unexpressed. Ellicott catches a distinction the English loses, since the verb here means to arbitrate and is not the verb for going to law used in the next breath. Barnes sharpens the taunt by naming the city, asking whether in a church at refined and enlightened Corinth, boasting of the number and qualifications of its intelligent members, not one is trusted; Wesley shortens it to admirers of wisdom with nobody wise enough to decide a cause. Calvin heads off an apparent contradiction, since Paul had written earlier that he did not mention their faults to shame them: by shaming them here he guards them from falling into reproach and is in fact promoting their honour. Robertson quotes the ascending scale from Robertson and Plummer, that disputes over the things of this life are bad, Christian going to law with Christian worse, and doing it before unbelievers worst of all; Clarke would expel from the church anyone refusing arbitration.

The word rendered a fault carries a metaphor the translation buries, and three commentators recover it differently. Robertson takes it from the vocabulary of the games and the field, where victory and defeat were the paired terms, so that to have lawsuits at all is already a defeat before any question of which court. Calvin derives it from weakness of mind, the condition of a man easily broken and irritated by injuries, and locates the fault accordingly in impatience rather than in the venue. Ellicott renders it a falling short of your privilege and dignity as Christians, the same word translated diminishing in Romans. Clarke simply lists four things wanting: peaceableness, brotherly love, mutual confidence, and reverence for God. Calvin then presses the hard objection, that on this reading no believer could ever maintain his rights before a magistrate, and refuses the easy escape offered by others, that a fault must lie somewhere because one of the two parties has a bad cause — that will not do, he says, since Paul faults not only the man who inflicts the injury but the man who will not endure it. Barnes limits the rebuke to heathen tribunals while conceding the same reasoning would bear against Christian courts.

The eighth verse reverses the charge, and the commentators register the shock in the grammar. Robertson marks the emphatic pronoun and the shift from the middle voice of suffering to the active voice of doing, so that these are the people doing the wronging and the robbing. Wesley reads the pair of verbs as a pair of methods, wrong done openly and defrauding done privately. Calvin builds an argument from the lesser to the greater: if a man sins by failing to bear an injury patiently, how much worse to inflict one, and worse again when the victim is a brother, since anyone who defrauds a stranger is doubly culpable and these had made sacred brotherhood a matter of no moment. Barnes states carefully what the aggravation is and is not, since injuring a Christian is in itself no worse than injuring another man; what the act shows is a deeper depravity, a man having overcome the tenderest ties before he could do it, which is why offences within a family are everywhere reckoned peculiarly atrocious. Clarke alone attaches the charge to a particular person, guessing that the fraud in view is the affair of the man who had taken his father's wife.
9:
Ellicott and Robertson both notice that the catalogue is bolted onto the lawsuit charge by a single word, since the unrighteous who shall not inherit are named with the same term used a verse earlier of the men doing the wrong. Robertson counts two lists divided by two different negatives and calls the whole a solemn roll call of the damned, even though some of the names on it were on the church roll at Corinth. Henry arranges the same names against the commandments, idolaters against the first and second, adulterers and their kind against the seventh, thieves and extortioners against the eighth, revilers against the ninth, the covetous and drunkards against the tenth. Clarke counts ten classes, says any one of them excludes a man, and declines to explain several of the terms at all. Barnes handles the hardest of them lexically, noting that the word occurs elsewhere in the New Testament only of the soft and costly clothing of the rich. Wesley draws the moral instead: these apparently harmless people are ranked with idolaters, which teaches that we are never secure from the greatest sins until we guard against the least.

On the sentence that follows, the small word some divides them. Gill takes it strictly: not all of them, and of those who were guilty not every one was guilty of everything, but among them the whole list had been committed. Robertson agrees, observing that the neuter plural registers the horror while the indefinite pronoun narrows the picture, and calls the clause a sharp home-thrust. Calvin argues the opposite, that the word is redundant in the Greek manner, added for ornament rather than restriction; he will not have the vices parcelled out to individuals but holds that human nature universally contains the seed of them all, and that until a man is renewed no one is exempt, one being inclined to cruelty, another to treachery, another to impurity, so that the difference between men is only which vices the Lord inwardly restrains from breaking out. He supports this from the way the same apostle piles up crimes in the opening chapters of Romans, where the throat is an open sepulchre and the feet swift to shed blood without every reader being sanguinary. Henry keeps to the plain encouragement, that some who are eminently good after conversion were as remarkably wicked before.

The three verbs at the close raise a question of order that nobody dodges. Henry calls it a rhetorical change of the natural order and passes on. Clarke denies flatly that anything is inverted and takes each term in turn: washed means baptized, with the washing of the body an emblem of the purifying of the soul; sanctified he derives from a root meaning separated from the earth, so that the man is parted from earthly things and joined to the living God; justified means brought into a state of favour with sins blotted out. Barnes reads them as a genuine sequence, washing for the beginning of the work in regeneration, sanctifying for the progress that follows and is plainly not yet complete in these readers, justifying for pardon. Robertson resolves the difficulty by the voice of the first verb, which is middle and not passive: the washing is the readers' own act in baptism, the outward expression of two divine acts that preceded it, and he cites Findlay that these twin conceptions commonly appear in the reverse order. Ellicott simply refuses to press the sequence at all, denying that the sanctification here means gradual progress in holiness.
12:
Whose words the maxim about all things being lawful is remains a live question. Ellicott thinks it a statement the apostle had himself made, dear to him and now misused, which he therefore repeats boldly before limiting it; Robertson agrees it is a proverb he had used at Corinth but not in the sense his opponents now give it. Calvin takes it as quoted from the Corinthians by anticipation, the reply they were accustomed to make when reproved. Barnes hears a common saying of those who palliated the indulgences in question. Clarke reconstructs two separate pleas behind it, that the offence of the man who had his father's wife was not contrary to the law as it then stood, and that since an idol is nothing a man may eat anywhere without defiling his conscience. Henry connects the maxim to the apostolic decree that had joined meats and fornication in one prohibition, and supposes the Corinthians reckoned themselves as free in the second as in the first, especially since their own laws did not condemn it. Ellicott adds, on Bengel's authority, that the singular pronoun is a form of moral maxim and no limitation of the principle to one man.

The answer turns on a play the English cannot carry, and three readers catch it separately. Ellicott points out that the word for lawful and the phrase for being brought under the power of are cognate, so the sense is that the writer will not let what is permitted to him become a law over him, and that there is such a thing as becoming the slave of liberty itself. Robertson calls it a conscious play on the same root and adds the wholesome hint to those who talk much of personal liberty. Chrysostom reaches the reversal without the grammar, by the turn he says the apostle is often fond of, bringing an argument clear round to its contrary: you say you have power to live luxuriously, but in doing so you are not exercising power over a thing so much as being subject to one, since a man who keeps the proper measure is master of his appetite and a man who exceeds it is its slave. Clarke states the test as a rule, that a man is brought under the power of anything he cannot give up. Wesley makes the same test inward, that if abstaining leaves you uneasy you are already under its power.

Ellicott sets out the reply to the second proverb as a formal argument in two halves: meats are an indifferent matter because they affect only the particular organ designed for them and because both shall perish together, while fornication is not, because it affects the man himself, who was not designed for it and who is immortal, so that its moral effect does not perish at his death. Barnes puts the first half plainly, that it is unworthy of a mind meant to live for ever to spend its thought on provision for what the grave will shortly destroy. Robertson identifies the fallacy in the parallel and quotes Findlay's sharp formulation, that the Lord Jesus and fornication contested for the bodies of Christian men, so that loyalty to the one meant renouncing the other. Calvin observes that the very decree of the apostles had placed fornication among things indifferent, which shows how generally it was then reckoned lawful. On the resurrection clause Calvin finds two arguments, that a body consecrated to Christ should not be profaned and that one destined for a blessed immortality should not be prostituted; Ellicott notes the phrase is among the few showing the writer did not expect the advent necessarily within his own lifetime.
15:
Chrysostom reads the return to the fornicator as a piece of deliberate strategy. The words are now addressed to those who had not committed the sin, but the offender is stung even so, his conscience thoroughly awakened and scourging him; and the method combines two things, since a man who only punishes a sin without showing its extreme lawlessness produces little effect by the chastisement, while one who only shames without terrifying does not keenly reach hardened minds. Robertson takes the figure of the members literally enough to set it against ancient and modern anthropologies alike, noting that the Stoics held the body to be common with the animals and only the reason to be like the gods, and adding a remark of his own about evolutionary defences of animalistic indulgence. He also weighs the verb for taking away, an old word meaning to snatch or carry off, and lets the horror of the sentence stand without softening it. Ellicott finds the same double act implied in the Greek, the taking of the members out of one union and the joining of them to another. Clarke, unwilling to print his more literal reading in English, sets it down in Latin instead and refers the reader to Schoettgen.

The quotation from Genesis creates a difficulty that Calvin refuses to paper over. Moses is speaking there not of a base and prohibited cohabitation but of the marriage connection which God blesses, and of a bond so close that it surpasses the tie between father and son; to cite it as proof that two fornicators become one flesh is to turn it aside from its true meaning. He offers two ways out. Either the quotation confirms not the sentence immediately before it but the one that follows, so that the argument runs from husband and wife becoming one flesh to the believer becoming one spirit with the Lord; or else, since fornication is the corruption of a divine institution and so retains some resemblance to it, what is said of the one may be applied in part to the other — not to dignify it with praises belonging to marriage, but to express the heinousness of the sin. Barnes reaches the same caution more briefly, that the passage cannot be understood as having originally referred to illicit connections and is used here for illustration. Ellicott hears the opening exclamation as answering someone who resents the strength of what precedes and would like it watered down.

On the closing sentence Barnes calls the argument beautiful and states it as a comparison: the union of souls is more important, more lasting and more dear than any union of body with body can be, and since ours is with a Spirit wholly pure it is improper that so sacred a bond should be sundered for the other. Calvin argues the same shape from greater to less, that if a married man ought not to have illicit connection, the crime is far more heinous in believers, who are not merely one flesh with Christ but one spirit. Clarke turns it into a question that answers itself, since a man united to God receives his Spirit and becomes a partaker of the divine nature, and whoever could exchange such a relationship must be deeply fallen. Ellicott notes only that this explains in what sense we are the Lord's body. Gill spends his space instead on what the bond of that union is not: not the Spirit on Christ's side, since the Spirit received in regeneration is a fruit of union and an evidence of it rather than its ground; nor faith on ours, which is itself a gift, not of a uniting nature, and a grace of communion.
18:
The single imperative is treated as the whole of the counsel. Robertson notes the present tense and the abrupt asyndeton, making it the habit of fleeing without delay or parley. Clarke draws the line between kinds of temptation: some solicitations to sin may be reasoned with, but in this case if you parley you are undone, so reason not, but fly. Barnes develops the same distinction at length and more darkly, holding that there are sins a man may safely think about and this is not one of them, since the very passage of an impure thought through the mind leaves pollution behind it, an argument on the subject often defiles, a description ruins, and even the presentation of motives against it may fix the mind on the crime; safety lies only in refusing to entertain the thought, a victory won by flight and a conquest by retreat. Wesley compresses the whole to three adverbial phrases, with speed, with abhorrence, and with all your might. Clarke adds a claim about consequences in this life, that such connections are married to death by the just judgment of God and that those given to them cannot live out half their days.

The claim that every other sin is outside the body raises an objection nobody ignores. Calvin states it squarely, that the body is defiled by theft and murder and drunkenness too, hands with blood and the whole body with drink; he reports that some escape the difficulty by rendering the disputed word differently, calls that more ingenious than solid, and observes that their reading would let idolatry qualify as well, since a man prostrate before an idol also sins against his connection with Christ. His own answer is comparative: other vices dishonour the body but the defilement does not remain impressed upon it in the same way. Barnes takes the same comparative line, that ordinary sins do not immediately and directly waste the body's energies. Robertson agrees that gluttony and drunkenness are wrought on the body but not within it in the same sense, and finds the dominant idea elsewhere, that here the body is at once the instrument of the sin and the thing damaged by it. Ellicott reads body throughout as the whole human nature, so that other sins profane only the outer courts of the temple while this one penetrates to the holy of holies.

Robertson supplies the local fact that makes the temple image bite: at Corinth stood the shrine of Aphrodite, where fornication counted as consecration rather than desecration and the prostitutes served as priestesses, so that a man was invited to worship the goddess by the act. He adds that the argument admits no double standard, unchastity being dishonour in both sexes. Wesley draws a doctrinal inference from the wording, that what is elsewhere called the temple of God is here called the temple of the Holy Ghost, which plainly shows the Holy Ghost to be the living God. On the price, Calvin weighs whether the word means simply that something cost a price or, adverbially, that it cost dearly, and prefers the second, comparing the precious blood of the lamb without blemish. Barnes insists at length that the language is figurative and not a commercial transaction, since the matter belongs to moral government rather than to trade. Clarke reports that the closing clause about the spirit is absent from many manuscripts, versions and fathers, and that almost every critic of note thinks it spurious, though the sense stands either way; Robertson agrees the words are late and not genuine.
